title: Origins and History
description: Signature basketball begins in a winter gym in Springfield, where James Naismith, needing an indoor game in December 1891, nailed peach baskets to a balcony and wrote thirteen rules. The rules' genius was restraint: no running with the ball, no shouldering opponents, and scoring by throwing into a basket, which made skill, not force, the game's currency. Early players had to climb for the ball after every basket, since the peach baskets kept their bottoms, until open nets let the ball fall through. From schools and the YMCA the game spread worldwide, reaching the Olympics in 1936 and professional leagues led by the NBA, without losing the shape Naismith gave it: fast, high-scoring, and open to anyone with a ball and a hoop.

history: Basketball was invented in December 1891 in Springfield, Massachusetts, by James Naismith, who nailed peach baskets to a gym balcony.
competitions: The sport spread through schools and colleges, became Olympic in 1936, and grew into professional leagues worldwide, led by the NBA.
rules: Naismith's original thirteen rules banned running with the ball and physical contact, principles that remain in the modern game.

title: Rules and the Court
description: Signature basketball law fits on a court: five per side, a hoop ten feet high, and points by shooting through it, two inside the arc, three beyond, one from the free-throw line. The dribble is the game's defining constraint, because a player who stops dribbling must pass or shoot, which forces constant movement and decision-making. The shot clock, twenty-four seconds under FIBA rules, stops a team from holding the ball indefinitely and keeps the pace high. Quarters, ten minutes under FIBA and twelve under the NBA, with overtime for ties, give the game a rhythm of bursts and breaks. Fouls cost free throws or possession, and too many fouls remove a player, so discipline is part of skill.

rules: Two teams of five play four quarters, score by shooting into a hoop 3.05 metres high, and win by scoring more points, with two points for field goals and three beyond the arc.
history: The court, hoop height, and shot clock have been standardised by federations, with FIBA and NBA rules differing in detail.
techniques: Players must dribble to move with the ball, and violations include travelling, double dribble, and shot-clock expiry.

title: Positions
description: Signature positions are five jobs, not five cages: point guard runs the offence, shooting guard scores from outside, small forward does a bit of everything, power forward works near the basket, and centre guards the rim. The point guard's job is the most cerebral, setting up teammates and reading defences, while the centre's job is the most physical, rebounding and protecting the basket. Modern play blurs the lines, with centres shooting threes and guards posting up, but the shorthand survives because it still describes what a lineup needs: someone to create, someone to score, someone to rebound, and someone to defend the rim. A good lineup balances those needs, whatever the labels on the players.

techniques: Point guard, shooting guard, small forward, power forward, and centre each have distinct roles, though modern play is increasingly positionless.
training: Guards train ball-handling and passing, forwards train versatility, and centres train post play, rebounding, and rim protection.
rules: Positions are conventions, not rules: any player may shoot, pass, or defend anywhere, and coaches assign roles to suit their roster.

title: Shooting
description: Signature shooting is a family of forms with shared keys: balanced feet, a smooth release, a high arc, and a wrist that follows through toward the basket. The jump shot is the outside standard, rising and releasing high over a defender; the layup is the close-range finisher, laid off the backboard with one hand; the free throw is the unguarded test of routine under pressure; and the three-pointer, worth an extra point beyond the arc, stretches defences and changes game plans. Form is built by repetition, then tested by movement, tiredness, and a closing defender, because game shooting is never as clean as practice shooting. The best shooters are not those with the prettiest form but those whose form survives pressure.

techniques: Jump shots, layups, free throws, three-pointers, and bank shots use different mechanics, with follow-through, balance, and arc as common keys.
training: Shooting practice builds form through repetition, then adds movement, fatigue, and defensive pressure to match game conditions.
statistics: Field-goal percentage, three-point percentage, and free-throw percentage measure shooting efficiency.

title: Dribbling and Ball-Handling
description: Signature ball-handling is movement with a bouncing ball: low, controlled, and protected by the body, with changes of pace that wrong-foot defenders. The crossover switches hands in front, the behind-the-back and between-the-legs moves hide the ball from a reaching defender, and the spin turns past an opponent who has committed to one side. The rule that shapes it all is simple: stop dribbling and you must pass or shoot, since starting again is a double dribble, so every move must end in a decision. Practising with both hands, at speed, and under pressure is what turns a drill move into a game move, because a defender will not wait politely while a player shows off a dribble.

techniques: Crossovers, behind-the-back, between-the-legs, and spin moves beat defenders, with low dribbles, change of pace, and protection of the ball as basics.
rules: A player must dribble continuously to move with the ball; stopping and starting again is a double-dribble violation.
training: Ball-handling drills build control with both hands, at speed, and under defensive pressure.

title: Passing
description: Signature passing is the fastest way to move a ball: faster than any dribble, and harder for a defence to chase. The chest pass is the workhorse, firm and direct; the bounce pass ducks under reaching hands; the overhead pass clears tall defenders and launches breaks; and the no-look pass deceives by looking one way and throwing another. The skill is not just throwing but anticipating: a pass must arrive where a teammate will be, at the moment they get there, which means reading cuts before they happen. Assists credit the passer who creates a score, and the best teams pass until the defence breaks, because a ball moved twice is a defence moved twice.

techniques: Chest passes, bounce passes, overhead passes, and no-look passes move the ball faster than any dribble, with timing and accuracy as keys.
training: Passing drills practise accuracy on the move, passing under pressure, and reading a teammate's cut before it happens.
statistics: Assists, passes leading directly to a score, measure a player's playmaking contribution.

title: Defense
description: Signature defence is five players moving as one: stance low, feet sliding, hands active, and voices calling screens and cuts. Man-to-man defence assigns each defender an opponent and demands that they stay goal-side and contest without fouling; zone defence assigns areas and demands that the zone shifts as the ball moves, protecting the basket at the cost of conceding some outside shots. Pressing defends the full court to force turnovers, and switching on screens avoids mismatches, but both need communication to work. Help defence is the test: when one defender is beaten, another must step in, and the team must rotate to cover whoever is left open. A defence that talks and rotates is hard to score on, whatever system it plays.

techniques: Man-to-man defence, zone defence, pressing, and switching cover different threats, with stance, footwork, and communication as basics.
rules: Defenders may not hold, push, or impede illegally; fouls give the offence free throws or possession depending on the rules and foul count.
training: Defensive drills practise slides, closeouts, help defence, and rotations, since defence is a five-player responsibility.

title: Rebounding
description: Signature rebounding is the game's second chance: a defensive board ends an opponent's possession, an offensive board creates another one, and a putback turns a miss into points in a single motion. Boxing out is the foundation, using the body to seal an opponent away from the basket, and timing is the rest, jumping to meet the ball at its peak rather than after it has fallen. Two hands secure the ball, because a one-handed tip is a gamble and a two-handed grab is a possession. Height helps, but positioning and effort help more: the player who wants the rebound, moves first, and jumps at the right moment will beat a taller player who merely watches. Close games are often rebounding games, decided by who wants the ball more after a miss.

techniques: Boxing out, timing the jump, and securing the ball with two hands are rebounding fundamentals, with offensive and defensive rebounds as distinct skills.
training: Rebounding drills practise positioning, contact, and second efforts, since rebounds often decide close games.
statistics: Rebounds are counted per player and team, with offensive rebounds giving extra scoring chances.

title: Fast Break
description: Signature fast break is defence turned into offence in seconds: a rebound or steal, an outlet pass, and teammates sprinting into lanes before the defence can set. The outlet is the spark, because a quick pass up the middle beats a dribble every time, and lane discipline is the shape, with runners wide and ahead of the ball so the handler always has an option. The handler's read decides the finish: drive if the lane is open, pass if a defender commits, and never force a contested shot when a teammate is free. Breaks reward rebounding and passing more than individual speed, since a team that moves the ball moves faster than any single sprinter. It is basketball at its most joyful: a stop, a sprint, and a score before the defence has caught its breath.

training: Break drills practise outlet passing, lane discipline, and decision-making at speed, since a break lasts only seconds.
rules: No special rules govern fast breaks; the same travelling, foul, and out-of-bounds rules apply at full speed.

title: Half-Court Offense
description: Signature half-court offence is patience with a plan: the defence is set, so the offence must move it. The pick-and-roll is the engine, a screen that frees the handler to drive, shoot, or feed the rolling screener, and off-ball screens free shooters while spacing keeps help defenders honest. Ball movement is the method: pass, cut, screen, and pass again until a defender is a step late, and then take the open shot that results. Forcing a contested shot early wastes the possession, while waiting for a high-percentage chance, even for several passes, wins games over a season. Late-clock execution is the final test, when a team needs one good look and one player brave enough to take it.

techniques: Pick-and-roll, off-ball screens, spacing, and ball movement create shots against a set defence, with patience and execution as keys.
training: Half-court drills practise set plays, reads against different defences, and late-clock execution.
statistics: Points per possession in the half court measure how efficiently a team scores when it cannot run.

title: Training and Conditioning
description: Signature basketball conditioning is built for a game that asks for everything at once: sprint, stop, jump, land, and shoot, then do it again. Training mixes skill work with scrimmages, so technique is practised under fatigue rather than only fresh, and strength work protects knees and ankles, the joints that absorb every landing. Load is a season-long plan: build early, maintain through competition, and ease before key games, because a tired team loses close games in the fourth quarter. Landing technique deserves special attention, since a soft, balanced landing prevents the injuries that end seasons. Position details differ, but the demand is shared: be able to play hard, late, and well.

safety: Warm-ups, ankle and knee prevention, and load management reduce injuries, with jumping and landing technique a focus.
techniques: Conditioning demands include repeated sprints, lateral movement, jumping, and endurance, with position-specific programmes.

title: Refereeing
description: Signature refereeing is coverage at speed: two or three officials rotating to see the whole court, calling violations and fouls while players sprint, jump, and collide. Table officials carry the bookkeeping, score, fouls, clocks, and shot clock, while video review, where used, settles only the questions a human eye cannot settle in real time, such as a buzzer-beater or a foot on the three-point line. Positioning is the referee's craft, because a call made from the wrong angle is a guess, and clear signals are its language, telling players, coaches, and crowds what was decided and why. Fitness matters as much as rules knowledge, since an official who cannot keep up cannot be where the play is.

techniques: Officials train in positioning, signals, communication, and fitness, and rotate positions to cover the whole court.
history: Officiating has grown with the game, with two- and three-person crews standard at higher levels and video review in major competitions.

title: Major Leagues and Competitions
description: Signature competitions give basketball its seasons and its summits: leagues that reward consistency, and tournaments that reward nerve. The NBA, founded in 1946, sets the professional standard, with a long regular season and best-of-seven playoff series; the WNBA, founded in 1996, is the women's professional summit; and the EuroLeague gathers Europe's top clubs. Internationally, the FIBA World Cup, begun in 1950, and Olympic basketball, played since 1936, let national teams chase gold. A league champion proves itself over months, a tournament champion over days, and both kinds of champion matter, because basketball, like every team sport, needs both the marathon and the sprint.

competitions: The NBA, WNBA, EuroLeague, and FIBA World Cup and Olympic tournaments are basketball's premier competitions.
history: The NBA was founded in 1946, the WNBA in 1996, and the FIBA World Cup began in 1950, with Olympic basketball since 1936.
rules: Leagues use regular seasons followed by playoffs, with series deciding champions, while tournaments use group stages and knockouts.

title: Women's Basketball
description: Signature women's basketball is nearly as old as basketball itself: the first women's college game came in 1893, two years after Springfield, which means women have played this game almost from its birth. Olympic women's basketball began in 1976, the WNBA in 1996 gave it a professional home, and the Women's World Cup crowns its world champions. The game needs no separate rulebook: same court, same tactics, same athleticism, with a slightly smaller ball in most competitions. Its growth in audiences and participation is recent and rapid, and the remaining work is familiar across sport: pay, facilities, and coverage brought up to the standard the players have already set on the court.

competitions: The WNBA, Olympic women's basketball, and the FIBA Women's World Cup are the premier women's competitions.
statistics: Audiences and participation for women's basketball have grown sharply, though pay and coverage gaps remain in many leagues.

title: 3x3 Basketball
description: Signature 3x3 is basketball stripped to its essentials: three per side, one basket, a half court, and a twelve-second clock that never lets the game stall. First to twenty-one, or ahead after ten minutes, wins, and the small court means every player must score, defend, and rebound, with nowhere to hide. Born from streetball and pickup games, it became a FIBA sport and an Olympic event at Tokyo 2020, keeping its festival feel: outdoor courts, music, and tournaments where anyone can enter. It is the most accessible form of basketball, because it needs only half a court, one hoop, and six players, and it teaches the whole game in miniature.

history: 3x3 grew from streetball and pickup games into a FIBA-governed sport and an Olympic event, debuting at Tokyo 2020.
techniques: Quick decisions, one-on-one skill, and outside shooting matter most, with no coaches on the sideline during play in many events.

title: Wheelchair Basketball
description: Signature wheelchair basketball is the running game, adapted with care and played at full intensity: five per side, a standard court, a standard hoop, and chairs built for speed and turning. Classification is the key adaptation, assigning points by functional ability and capping a team's on-court total, so that lineups balance different abilities fairly. Chair skills, pushing, turning, picking, and stopping, are as fundamental as dribbling, and contact rules govern chair-to-chair play as foul rules govern body contact in the running game. Born from post-war rehabilitation sport, it is now a Paralympic centrepiece, proof that basketball's shape, five players, a ball, a hoop, survives translation to a chair without losing its speed or its drama.
